Question: How can natural selection design anything?
Old_Answer: Imagine you're outside on a nice summer evening, walking through the woods with a few friends. Suddenly, you hear a buzzing in the distance. You turn around until you find the source: a particularly noisy mosquito headed straight toward you. You slam your hands together and kill it. You're on high alert now; you hate mosquito bites. You warn your friends that they're coming out. Another mosquito sloppily lands on your arm, hard enough for you to feel it. One swift slap and it's nothing but a corpse. You and your friends keep walking and swatting mosquitoes. Suddenly, you feel a pinching sensation on your left calf. You look down and find a mosquito sucking up your blood. You kill it, then curse to yourself since you've already been bitten. But it's only one time, so what's the harm? You and your friends make it back to the great indoors and go to sleep. The next morning you all wake up covered in mosquito bites. “How??” You all wonder. “We killed all of the mosquitoes!” Turns out, the mosquitoes who were quiet, the mosquitoes who were gentle, the mosquitoes whose bites didn't hurt, were the ones that survived. These mosquitoes are the ones who get to reproduce a higher percent of the time than the loud, sloppy, and painful ones. Even if it's only 1% more often, imagine that process stretched out over thousands or even millions of years. That 1% better chance means there’s 1% more of that kind of mosquito the next season, which leads to another 1% more the next, etc etc. After a couple million years, there's only the best mosquitoes left. And then we won't hear any of them coming.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Natural selection doesn’t “design” in the way we think of a designer creating something with intention. It’s more like a filtering process that sifts through variations in traits within a population. Imagine a vast ocean filled with countless fish, each with slightly different colors, sizes, and swimming abilities. Some fish are better at evading predators, while others are more efficient at finding food. Over time, those that survive and reproduce pass on their advantageous traits to the next generation. This isn’t a conscious design; it’s a natural consequence of survival and reproduction. Think of it as a game of chance where the players are constantly adapting to their environment. The traits that help individuals thrive become more common, while those that don’t fade away. This process can lead to the emergence of complex structures and behaviors, but it’s all driven by random mutations and environmental pressures, not a blueprint. Take the eye, for example. It didn’t appear overnight as a fully formed organ. Instead, it evolved gradually from simple light-sensitive cells to the intricate structures we see today. Each step along the way provided some advantage, however small, that contributed to the survival of the organism. So, in essence, natural selection is less about design and more about the relentless march of adaptation, where the “design” is simply the result of countless generations of trial and error. Life is a messy, chaotic process, and that’s what makes it so fascinating.

Question: What is something you wish people would stop saying?
Old_Answer: Today, I wish people (especially teenagers) would stop saying “Go vote!” I wrote an answer a while back about how nothing you say on the internet about politics matters until you put it into practice and vote. And that’s true. But there’s voting, and then there’s whipping yourself up into a frenzy over people voting or not voting. This is a story I screenshotted from some girl I happen to follow. I went ahead and scribbled/added the emoji to protect her privacy. It was one of three pictures of her pointing a gun at a camera and telling people to vote. And after the third picture? I laughed a little to myself about this girl feeling the need to insert her gun control opinion into her voting plea, but mostly I just felt annoyed. These thousands (or millions) of young people around the country aren’t saying “go vote” because they want young people to express their views. They’re saying “go vote” because they think young people will vote the same way they do. And that’s fine, morally. It’s just annoying. No one needs a hundred reminders on the day of the elections to go vote - the people who were gonna vote had already decided they would, and the people who weren’t aren’t gonna be persuaded by an angry last-minute plea for them to get to the polls (“or die”). What you’re really doing is virtue signaling. “I’m woke! I’m a member of The Resistance! I don’t just vote, I mobilize other people to vote!” Yeah, you’re a real civil rights activist for putting “Go vote!” on your Instagram story. At the end of the day, it’s just another election. The sun will rise tomorrow, the birds will chirp, people will go to work, and the world will keep on spinning, like it has for the last 4 1/2 billion years. Feel free to vote, but calm the hell down.

Instead of offering empty platitudes, we should focus on being present and supportive. Listen to people’s struggles, validate their feelings, and help them navigate through the messiness of life. Life isn’t a neatly wrapped package with a bow on top; it’s messy, complicated, and often unfair. We need to acknowledge that and allow people to feel their emotions without trying to sugarcoat their experiences. Question: Would you care if Trump was assassinated? The majority of sensible people would prefer him gone.
Old_Answer: Yes, because that is not the basis on which we decide to murder someone. I’m not a frothing-at-the-mouth Trump fan, although I do like a lot of his politics. But let’s set aside political leanings here. And let’s set aside the fact that the country would be thrown into chaos for weeks (likely months) if this were to actually happen (which means everyone would end up caring, sensible or not). Let’s take a look at why you should care if Trump is assassinated, regardless of your political leanings or opinions of him. You could’ve phrased your question as “Would you care if Trump was assassinated?” But you added a second part to it. A part that heavily implies that, since “the majority of sensible people” want him gone, his assassination wouldn’t really matter. “Sensible people” is a subjective term. Who gets to define what it means to be a sensible person? Ok, maybe you’d argue that the majority of a population gets to define it. Fair enough. You’ve just identified the greatest danger of democracy: Mob rule. Let’s say 90% of the country decided tomorrow that they wanted you dead. Would they have the right to kill you? And if you said no, would it change your mind if I told you that “the majority of sensible people” are part of that 90%? Trump is, fundamentally, a human being. Just like you. Just like me. Just like every other human being who has ever existed or ever will exist. In our legal system, violent force against another is only justified in self-defence or in the defence of other’s lives. Trump is not a murderer. Despite what Buzzfeed might have you believe, Trump is not “literally Hitler.” If a person were to assassinate Trump, they should face the full prosecution of the law. They are subject to the same standard we are all subject to. Now you might be thinking, “Yeah yeah, it’s illegal and rule of law matters and all that. But why should I care if Trump is assassinated?” You should care because you’re a citizen of this country. You, just like me, are responsible for supporting the rule of law in this country. Why? Because it benefits us. Having laws that protect us against murder is a good thing that we should all strive to enforce. And if that STILL isn’t enough for you, Trump is a human being. I get that you don’t know him personally, and I get that you don’t like him. But he’s still a human being. He has a family. He has hopes and dreams. And most importantly, he has an intrinsic right to life. You should care about that right to life being violated. We all should. Because it doesn’t take much for society to become rampantly murderous if we don’t.
